ticket.title: miter audit should refuse a commit deleting tracked .gaugeblock state without citing a decision record
ticket.description:
The rule that would have prevented this whole line of work, and the last refusal owed on storypole SP-40.

WHAT HAPPENED: on 2026-11-06 ten repositories each committed chore(storypole): retire the legacy repo-local ledger, deleting their .storypole/ledger.jsonl and keeping the bytes at the suite root. It read as routine hygiene. Nobody asked why the files had frozen, and the answer - because nothing wrote to them, because write routing was never wired - was the actual defect. Days of work were spent rediscovering it.

WHAT THE RULE SHOULD DO: a commit that deletes tracked files under .gaugeblock/ must cite a decision record (docs/decisions/NNNN-*.md or an ADR-NNNN reference) in its message. Requiring the ADR forces the sentence that exposes the circularity: an ADR has to say why the state is superseded, and because-nothing-writes-to-it is a statement that invites a second look.

WHERE: src/cli/audit_paths.rs alongside audit_layout_adoption, so it runs in the same --paths gate every repository chain already calls.

THE HARD PART: the historical commits are already in ten repositories, so a naive rule reports violations from day one and blocks every chain. It needs a baseline - commits reachable from a recorded marker, or an allowlist beside layers-allowlist.toml naming each accepted deletion with its justification. The allowlist is probably right: ten entries, each stating why the deletion was correct, is a durable record rather than an exemption.

TESTS: a fixture repository with a deletion that cites an ADR (passes), one that does not (fails naming the commit), and one that is allowlisted (passes).

PLACEMENT QUESTIONED 2026-11-08, and the answer is not as clean as the ticket implied.

Raised: audit is a report, verify has gates - so should this rule live in miter verify instead?

MEASURED: neither verb is named for what it does.
  - `miter verify` is "run isolated compiler verification on the workspace or crate". A commit-message policy is
    not a compiler check, and it is repository-scoped where verify is crate-scoped.
  - `miter audit` is described as a scan that flags files over a line limit, and it exits non-zero - every
    repository chain already depends on that exit code, and it blocked work today when a file reached 250 lines.

So audit is a gate wearing a report's name, and the criticism is correct about the vocabulary.

RECOMMENDATION: implement in `audit --paths`, alongside audit_layout_adoption, because the two existing policy
rules already live there and all eleven chains call it; a policy rule in `verify` would be the only one of its kind
and would answer a repo-wide question per crate.

THE VOCABULARY DECISION IS THIS TICKET'S, and should be made once rather than per rule:
  a) accept `audit` as the gate surface and say so in its help text - one paragraph;
  b) split report from gate (audit prints and exits 0, a gate verb exits non-zero) and update eleven chains plus
     .gaugeblock/config.toml - mechanical, but must cover the three existing rules at the same time.
Either is fine; adding a fourth rule without choosing is not.

DECIDED BY EVIDENCE 2026-11-08: `audit`, not `verify`.

Counted in .gaugeblock/config.toml, which holds all thirteen verification chains:
  - `miter audit --path . --threshold 250 --paths` appears in every chain;
  - `miter verify` appears ZERO times.

So the vocabulary question has a factual answer. `verify` is not a gate surface in this suite at all: it is the
compiler step that storypole's own verification invokes to produce a receipt. `audit` is what every chain actually
gates on, together with `miter contracts`, `outfeed lockfiles` and `chalkline docs check`.

Therefore this rule goes in `audit --paths`, and the remaining vocabulary work is smaller than option (b) implied: it
is not a split between report and gate, it is making `miter audit`'s help text say that it exits non-zero and that
`--paths` runs the policy gates. One paragraph, no chain changes.

The criticism was still worth making: a command described as a scan, depended on as a gate, is a trap for whoever
reads the help text instead of the chains.

receipt.command: cargo fmt --all -- --check && cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings && cargo nextest run --workspace && miter audit --path . --threshold 250 --paths && chalkline docs check -d miter
